title: The Daodejing: The Way That Cannot Be Named
bigQuestion: How can a short book that says its subject cannot be put into words shape a philosophy, a religion, and the arts of painting, medicine and movement?

story.title: The Hollow in the Temple Step
story.kicker: A soft drip of rainwater, a worn stone, and an old story about a teacher who wrote one book at a border gate.
paragraphs: Climb the stone stairs of an old mountain temple in China and look closely at the lowest step beneath the eaves. In its center is a smooth hollow about the size of a rice bowl. No chisel made it. For centuries, rain has run off the curved roof tiles and dripped onto the same spot, one drop at a time. The stone is hard and the water is soft, yet the water has won. A priest sweeping the courtyard might point to it and recall a teaching from an ancient book: nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down what is hard.

That book is the Daodejing, and Chinese tradition tells a story about how it came to be written. Its author, the story says, was an old archivist at the court of the Zhou kings, called Laozi, the Old Master. Seeing the kingdom decline, he decided to leave and head west. At the border pass, the gatekeeper recognized a wise man and would not let him go until he wrote down what he knew. So Laozi sat and wrote about five thousand characters in two parts. Then he rode through the gate, and no one knows where he went. Later paintings show him riding a water buffalo.

The book he left is strange and short. It praises the empty space inside a bowl, the low places where water gathers, the newborn child who is soft and the ruler whom people barely notice. It says that the Way that can be spoken of is not the lasting Way. It speaks in paradoxes and never tells a story or names a person. Over two thousand years it has been read by emperors and hermits, generals and poets, priests in temples and, in modern times, readers around the world in hundreds of translations.

This chapter reads that book and the stories of Zhuangzi, the second great Daoist voice. It then follows Daoism as a religion, with its priests, temples, scriptures and hopes for long life, and looks at how Daoist ideas shaped painting, medicine and martial arts. It also shows how Daoism has lived beside Confucianism and Buddhism, often in the same families. In parks from Beijing to Chicago, people practice tai chi in the morning, moving slowly and softly, like water.
story.think: The story of Laozi at the pass cannot be confirmed, yet it has been told for over two thousand years. What might a community gain from telling it, and how should a student of religion treat such a story?

sections.title: The Old Master and His Book

lessons.title: Laozi and the Gatekeeper
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition says Laozi wrote the Daodejing, but scholars see it as a collection that took shape over time and was circulating by about 300 BCE.
reading: The earliest account of Laozi comes from the historian Sima Qian, who wrote his Records of the Grand Historian around 100 BCE. He says that *Laozi*, the Old Master, was named Li Er and kept the archives at the Zhou court. Confucius once visited him to ask about ritual and came away comparing him to a dragon, a creature no one can grasp. Seeing the Zhou in decline, Laozi left for the west. At the border pass, the gatekeeper Yin Xi asked him to write down his teaching first. Laozi wrote a book in two parts of about five thousand characters, then departed.

Sima Qian himself was unsure of the details. In the same passage he mentions two other men who might have been Laozi, and he notes reports that the Old Master lived more than 160 years. Modern historians treat the story as *legend*: a traditional account whose details cannot be confirmed. Many doubt that a single author wrote the book at all. Its short chapters look like sayings gathered, edited and arranged over time, and the book names no people, places or events that would date it.

Archaeology has sharpened the picture. In 1973, two copies of the book written on silk were found in a tomb at *Mawangdui*, sealed in 168 BCE. In 1993, bamboo slips found in a tomb at *Guodian*, sealed around 300 BCE, turned out to hold passages matching about a third of the book's chapters, sometimes in a different order. So much of the text was circulating by about 300 BCE, and its shape was still changing. The version most people read today, in 81 chapters, follows the edition of the scholar Wang Bi (226–249 CE).

For many Daoists, the story carries meaning beyond dates. Religious Daoism came to honor Laozi as a divine being, Taishang Laojun, the Most High Lord Lao, who appears in many ages to teach. Historians read the name as a label attached to a book. Both groups agree on the book's influence. Apply the toolkit from the start of this course: the author is uncertain, the audience seems to be rulers and seekers, and the purpose is to point toward a Way that words cannot fully hold.

words.d: the Old Master; by tradition the author of the Daodejing and an older contemporary of Confucius
a traditional story about the past whose details cannot be confirmed by historical evidence
a tomb site in Hunan, sealed in 168 BCE, where two silk copies of the Daodejing were found in 1973
a tomb site in Hubei, sealed about 300 BCE, where the earliest known Daodejing passages were found in 1993

look.title: Dating a Book Without a Date
look.cite: traditional dates and archaeological dating in standard histories of early China
look.prompt: Tradition makes Laozi older than Confucius. How many years after Confucius's death do the earliest known manuscripts date? What do the tombs prove, and what can they not prove?

check.q: Who wrote the earliest surviving account of Laozi's life?
check.why: The historian Sima Qian told Laozi's story in his Records of the Grand Historian around 100 BCE.

check.q: What did the bamboo slips found at Guodian show?
choices: That the book was first written after 1000 CE
That much of the text was circulating by about 300 BCE
That the book was first written in Sanskrit
check.why: The Guodian tomb, sealed about 300 BCE, held passages matching about a third of the chapters.

check.q: In the traditional story, who asked Laozi to write down his teaching?
check.why: Sima Qian says the keeper of the border pass, Yin Xi, asked Laozi to write before he left.

lessons.title: Reading a Book of Paradox
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing is a short book of 81 poetic chapters that teaches through paradox, so every translation of it, including Legge's, is an interpretation.
reading: The whole *Daodejing* fits on a few pages: about five thousand Chinese characters in 81 short chapters. The first 37 chapters are traditionally called the Dao section and the rest the De section, and the title joins them: dao, the Way; de, virtue or power; jing, classic. Most chapters are rhymed verse, dense and compressed. Unlike the Analects, it has no named speakers, no students and no stories. A voice simply speaks to the reader, often holding up the sage, the wise ruler, as a model.

The book teaches through *paradox*, statements that seem to contradict themselves but point to something true. The soft overcomes the hard. Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know. The sage puts himself last and so finds himself first. Returning, the book says, is the movement of the Dao. A paradox stops a reader who is moving too fast and forces a second look, which may be exactly its purpose.

Compressed classical Chinese allows many readings, so translations differ widely. The Daodejing is among the most translated books in the world, with hundreds of English versions. This course quotes James Legge, whose version appeared in 1891 in the Sacred Books of the East, the series edited by Max Müller. Legge spelled the key word Tao and put in parentheses the words he added where the Chinese leaves meaning unstated. Those parentheses help a careful reader: they show where the translator is interpreting.

Spelling needs a note. Older English books wrote Tao, Tao Te Ching and Lao-tzu, using the *Wade-Giles* system of romanization. Today most scholars use *pinyin*, the system adopted in China in the 1950s, which gives Dao, Daodejing and Laozi. The Chinese words are the same; only the English letters differ. You will also see Daoism spelled Taoism. Both spellings name the same tradition, and in both the first sound is close to an English d.

words.d: the Classic of the Way and Its Power; the short book of 81 chapters traditionally credited to Laozi
a statement that seems to contradict itself but points to a truth, such as the soft overcomes the hard
an older system for writing Chinese in English letters, which gives Tao and Lao-tzu
the system for writing Chinese in English letters adopted in China in the 1950s, which gives Dao and Laozi

look.title: The Opening Lines
look.text: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 1, translated by James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891
look.prompt: If the Tao that can be named is not the lasting Tao, what is the book doing by naming it? What do Legge's words in parentheses tell you about his choices as a translator?

check.q: What do the three parts of the title Daodejing mean?
check.why: Dao is the Way, de is virtue or power, and jing means classic, joining the book's two sections.

check.q: Which line is an example of paradox from the Daodejing?
choices: Honor your father and your mother
At fifteen I set my mind on learning
Lead the people by laws and punishments
Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know
check.why: The line seems to contradict itself but points to a truth about knowledge, the Daodejing's typical method.

check.q: Why do Tao and Dao name the same thing?
choices: Tao is Japanese and Dao is Chinese
They are the same Chinese word spelled in two romanization systems
Tao is the religion and Dao is the philosophy
check.why: Wade-Giles writes Tao and pinyin writes Dao; the Chinese word is the same.

lessons.title: The Dao Beyond Names
lessons.mainIdea: In the Daodejing the Dao is the nameless source and pattern of all things, and de is the power a thing has when it follows its own Way.
reading: The word *Dao* means a road or path, and by extension a method or way of doing something. Confucius used it for the Way of the ancient kings, the right way to live and govern. The Daodejing pushes the word much further. Its Dao is the source from which heaven, earth and all things come, and the pattern they follow. The book calls it the Mother of all things and admits it does not know its true name. It calls it Dao, it says, only because it must call it something.

That is why the book opens by warning that the Dao that can be spoken of is not the lasting Dao. Words divide the world into this and that, high and low, good and bad. The Dao comes before those divisions. Chapter 42 gives a compressed account of how things arise: the Dao produces one, one produces two, two produce three, and three produce all things. Commentators have read the one as the undivided whole and the two as yin and yang, though the text itself does not say.

The Daodejing often points to the Dao through *emptiness*. Chapter 11 observes that thirty spokes meet at a wheel's hub, but the empty center is what makes the wheel useful. A clay pot is useful because of its hollow, and a room because of its open space. What is there brings benefit, the chapter concludes, but what is not there makes things usable. In the same way, the book describes the Dao as empty yet never used up, like a bellows or a valley.

The partner term is *de*, often translated virtue but closer to power or potency, the way people once spoke of the virtue of a medicine. De is the Dao at work in a particular thing, the power it has when it follows its nature. Scholars sometimes compare the Dao with Brahman in the Upanishads, studied earlier in this course. There is a difference from the God of the Hebrew Bible and the Qur'an: the Daodejing does not describe the Dao as a personal being who commands, judges or makes covenants.

words.d: the Way; in the Daodejing, the nameless source of all things and the pattern they follow
virtue or power; the potency of the Dao at work in a particular thing or person
open, unfilled space; in the Daodejing, what makes things usable and an image of the Dao

look.title: The Wheel, the Pot and the Room
look.text: Chapter 11 of the Daodejing, in paraphrase: Thirty spokes meet at one hub, but the empty space at the center makes the wheel work. Clay is shaped into a pot, but the hollow inside makes it useful. Doors and windows are cut into walls, but the empty space inside makes the room. So what is there gives benefit, and what is not there makes it usable.
look.prompt: Name one more everyday thing whose usefulness depends on empty space. What might it mean to say that a person, a conversation or a school day needs emptiness in order to work?

check.q: What does the ordinary Chinese word dao mean?
check.why: Dao means a road or path, and by extension a method; the Daodejing uses it for the source of all things.

check.q: According to chapter 11, what makes a wheel, a pot or a room useful?
check.why: The chapter says the empty hub, hollow and open space are what make each thing usable.

check.q: How does the Daodejing's Dao differ from God as described in the Hebrew Bible and the Qur'an?
choices: It is described as a king in heaven
It is worshiped only on a holy day
It is identified with Laozi himself
It is not described as a personal being who commands, judges or makes covenants
check.why: The Daodejing presents the Dao as a nameless source and pattern, not a personal lawgiver.

lessons.title: Wu Wei: Acting Without Forcing
lessons.mainIdea: Wu wei, action without forcing, is the Daodejing's ideal for the sage and the ruler: to act in step with the natural course of things rather than against it.
reading: A strong swimmer caught in a current does not fight it head on; she swims across it and lets it carry her toward shore. The Daodejing names this kind of effortless effectiveness *wu wei*, literally not-doing or non-action. It does not mean laziness or doing nothing. It means acting without forcing, grasping or showing off, so that things are accomplished the way plants grow, steadily and without strain. The book says the Dao does nothing, and yet nothing is left undone.

Wu wei belongs with *ziran*, naturalness, literally self-so: the way things are when left to their own course. A related image is *pu*, the uncarved block, wood before it is cut into tools. The book praises simplicity, few desires and contentment. In its view, the harder people strive for wealth, fame and cleverness, the more they lose their natural balance. Chapter 33 says that the person who is satisfied with his lot is rich.

The idea has a political side. Much of the Daodejing is addressed to rulers, and it advises a light touch. Chapter 60 says that governing a great state is like cooking a small fish: stir it too often and it falls apart. The book warns that the more laws and prohibitions there are, the more poverty and theft appear. The best rulers, it says, are those the people barely know exist; when their work is done, the people say it happened naturally.

Compare the Analects. Confucius also admired rule by example: the ruler as the north star, the people as grass bending in the wind. Both books reject government by force alone. But Confucius wanted more ritual, learning and deliberate effort, while the Daodejing criticizes humaneness and rightness when they are preached as programs and asks readers to let go instead. Historians often describe Chinese scholar-officials as Confucian in office and Daoist in retirement, holding both books at once.

words.d: non-action or not-forcing; acting in harmony with the natural course of things, without strain
naturalness, literally self-so; the way things are when left to follow their own course
the uncarved block; the Daodejing's image of simplicity, like wood before it is cut into tools

look.title: Nothing Left Undone
look.text: The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 37, translated by James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891
look.prompt: How can something that does nothing leave nothing undone? Give an example from nature, sports or music where the best result comes from not forcing.

check.q: What does wu wei mean in the Daodejing?
choices: Acting without forcing, in step with the natural course of things
The ritual bow before a ruler
check.why: Wu wei is not laziness; it is effective action without strain or grasping, like a plant growing.

check.q: What does chapter 60 compare governing a great state to?
check.why: Stir a small fish too often and it falls apart; a ruler who meddles too much harms the state.

check.q: What is pu, the uncarved block?
choices: An image of simplicity: wood before it is shaped into tools
The first chapter of the Zhuangzi
check.why: Pu stands for the simple, natural state that the Daodejing praises over cleverness and striving.

lessons.title: The Lesson of Water
lessons.mainIdea: The Daodejing uses water as its favorite image of the Dao: soft, low and yielding, yet able to wear away the hardest things.
reading: Return to the hollow in the temple step. Water is the Daodejing's favorite image of the Dao. Water benefits all things and does not compete with them. It flows to the low places people avoid. Chapter 78, in paraphrase, says that nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, yet nothing is better at overcoming what is hard and strong. The weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard, the chapter adds; everyone knows this, yet no one puts it into practice.

Water teaches several lessons at once. It teaches *yielding*: it gives way to whatever it meets and takes the shape of any container, yet it is never destroyed. It teaches lowness: according to chapter 66, rivers and seas rule the hundred valleys because they lie below them, and so a sage who would lead the people places himself beneath them. It teaches persistence: drop by drop, it cuts canyons. And it teaches stillness: muddy water, left alone, slowly becomes clear.

The book pairs water with other soft things. A newborn is soft and *supple*; the dead are stiff and hard. Green plants bend; dry ones snap. So, chapter 76 concludes, the stiff and hard are companions of death, and the soft and yielding are companions of life. Readers have taken this in many directions: as advice for rulers to avoid war, as a call to personal *humility*, and later as a principle of martial arts that meet force by giving way to it.

Other traditions also use water, and comparing them shows how one image can carry different meanings. In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Amos calls for justice to roll down like waters, a force that sweeps wrong away. In the Gospel of John, Jesus speaks of living water, meaning spiritual life. In the Daodejing, water's power lies in its softness and its willingness to go low. The same image, read in each tradition's context, teaches something different.

words.d: giving way instead of resisting; in the Daodejing, a strength that water shows
bending easily without breaking; the Daodejing links it to life, and stiffness to death
not putting oneself above others; in the Daodejing, taking the low place as water does

look.title: Like Water
look.text: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.
look.cite: Daodejing, chapter 8, translated by James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891
look.prompt: Name two qualities of water this chapter praises. Why would a book about the Dao praise taking the low place that all men dislike?

check.q: According to chapter 78 of the Daodejing, what can water do although it is soft?
choices: Overcome what is hard and strong
check.why: The chapter says nothing is softer than water, yet nothing is better at overcoming the hard and strong.

check.q: Why does chapter 66 say rivers and seas rule the hundred valleys?
choices: Because they are the largest bodies of water
Because they lie below the valleys
check.why: Their lowness lets all water flow to them; the sage likewise leads by placing himself beneath the people.

check.q: How does Amos's image of water differ from the Daodejing's?
choices: Amos praises water for going to the low place
The Daodejing uses water as a symbol of judgment
Both use water only for ritual washing
Amos pictures justice sweeping wrong away; the Daodejing praises water's softness and lowness
check.why: In Amos water is a mighty force of justice; in the Daodejing its power lies in yielding and going low.

lessons.title: Yin and Yang
lessons.mainIdea: Yin and yang are paired, complementary forces whose balance and constant change Chinese thought uses to describe everything that happens.
reading: Look at a hill in the late afternoon. One side is in shade, the other in sun. That is where the words come from: *yin* first meant the shady side of a hill and *yang* the sunny side. In Chinese thought they became names for two complementary forces present in everything. Yin is linked with darkness, cold, the moon, water, rest and receiving; yang with light, heat, the sun, fire, movement and acting. Traditional thought also paired yin with female and yang with male, a pairing many modern readers question.

Yin and yang are not good and evil. Neither is better, and neither can exist alone, just as a shady slope needs a sunny one. They are *complementary*, each completing the other, and they turn into each other: noon passes into evening, winter into spring. The familiar black-and-white circle, the taijitu, shows this. Each half swells as the other shrinks, and each holds a dot of the other at its heart. That diagram became common only in later centuries, but the idea behind it is far older.

Yin and yang belong to all Chinese thought, not to Daoism alone. The *Book of Changes*, the Yijing, one of the Five Classics honored by Confucians, builds 64 figures called hexagrams from broken yin lines and solid yang lines, and uses them for divination and reflection. Han scholars joined yin and yang to the *five phases*, wood, fire, earth, metal and water, to explain seasons, medicine and politics. Daoists gave these ideas a central place in meditation, medicine and ritual.

The pattern also runs through the Daodejing's paradoxes: being and non-being produce each other, difficult and easy complete each other, high and low depend on each other. Compare the dualism in Zoroastrian teaching, where a good spirit and an evil spirit struggle and the good is expected to win in the end. Yin-yang thinking looks for balance rather than victory. A healthy body, a good government or a well-lived day, in this view, keeps the two in harmony.

words.d: the dark, cool, receptive force in Chinese thought; first meant the shady side of a hill
the bright, warm, active force in Chinese thought; first meant the sunny side of a hill
completing each other; each needed to make a whole, as yin and yang are
the Yijing, a classic of 64 hexagrams made of yin and yang lines, used for divination and reflection
wood, fire, earth, metal and water; a Chinese system for explaining change in nature, the body and politics

look.title: Pairs in Motion
look.text: Day and night. Breathing in and breathing out. A wave rising and falling. Summer and winter. A teacher speaking and a class listening. A runner sprinting, then resting. In yin-yang thinking, each pair is not a fight between good and bad but two phases of one movement, each turning into the other.
look.prompt: Sort each pair into its yin side and its yang side and explain your choices. Then find a pair where calling one side better would be a mistake, and say why.

check.q: What did the words yin and yang first refer to?
choices: The shady and sunny sides of a hill
check.why: Yin first meant the shady slope and yang the sunny slope; the words later named two complementary forces.

check.q: How are yin and yang different from good and evil?
choices: Yin is always good and yang is always evil
They complete each other and change into each other, and neither is better
They appear only in Daoist texts
check.why: Yin and yang are complementary and always turning into each other; the goal is balance, not victory.

check.q: Which classic builds 64 hexagrams from broken and solid lines?
check.why: The Book of Changes, the Yijing, uses broken yin lines and solid yang lines to form its hexagrams.

lessons.title: The Butterfly and the Cook
lessons.mainIdea: The Zhuangzi teaches Daoist ideas through humorous and strange stories that question our certainties and show skill flowing from the Way.
reading: *Zhuangzi*, Master Zhuang (c. 369–286 BCE), is the second great Daoist voice. The book named after him has 33 chapters. Scholars generally treat the first seven, the *Inner Chapters*, as closest to Zhuangzi himself and the rest as the work of later followers; the scholar Guo Xiang, around 300 CE, edited the version that survives. Where the Daodejing speaks in terse verse, the Zhuangzi tells stories: talking trees, giant birds, disabled men wiser than kings, and Confucius himself, sometimes mocked and sometimes speaking like a Daoist.

The best-known story ends the second chapter. Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering happily, with no idea he was Zhuangzi. He woke, and there he was, Zhuangzi. But he could not tell whether he was Zhuangzi who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was Zhuangzi. The story calls this the *transformation of things*. It unsettles the sharp line between one self and another, and between waking and dreaming.

In the third chapter, *Cook Ding* carves an ox for a ruler. His knife moves to a rhythm like a dance, and the carcass falls apart as if by itself. He explains that at first he saw only the whole ox. Now he follows the natural joints and hollows and never hacks at bone. A good cook changes his knife every year and an ordinary cook every month, he says, but his has lasted nineteen years and is still sharp. The ruler says he has learned from this how to nourish life.

Both stories carry the Daodejing's ideas into daily life. Cook Ding is wu wei in action: skill so complete that it no longer strains. The butterfly questions the fixed categories the Daodejing warns about. Zhuangzi also enjoyed arguing with his friend Huizi, a logician. Watching fish in a river, Zhuangzi remarked how happy they were. Huizi asked how he could know, since he was not a fish. Zhuangzi asked how Huizi could know what he knew, since Huizi was not Zhuangzi. Zhuangzi gets a clever last word, and readers still argue over who won.

words.d: Master Zhuang (c. 369–286 BCE), Daoist thinker, and the book of stories named after him
the first seven chapters of the Zhuangzi, which scholars see as closest to Zhuangzi himself
the Zhuangzi's name for the endless changing of one thing into another, as in the butterfly dream
the butcher in the Zhuangzi whose effortless carving shows skill that follows the natural Way

look.title: The Butterfly Dream
look.text: Once Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, flitting about and enjoying itself, not knowing it was Zhuangzi. Suddenly he woke, and there he was, plainly Zhuangzi. He did not know whether he was Zhuangzi who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming that it was Zhuangzi. Yet between Zhuangzi and a butterfly there must be some difference. This is called the transformation of things.
look.cite: Zhuangzi, end of chapter 2, in paraphrase; compare Legge's translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891
look.prompt: The story says there must be some difference, then calls it the transformation of things. What is the story asking you to doubt, and what does it leave in place?

check.q: Which part of the Zhuangzi do scholars treat as closest to Zhuangzi himself?
choices: The Inner Chapters, the first seven
check.why: Scholars generally see the Inner Chapters as Zhuangzi's own and the later chapters as the work of followers.

check.q: Why has Cook Ding's knife stayed sharp for nineteen years?
choices: He follows the natural joints and hollows instead of hacking at bone
check.why: Cook Ding works with the ox's natural structure, a picture of wu wei, so his blade never strikes bone.

check.q: How does the Zhuangzi's style differ from the Daodejing's?
choices: It contains no mention of Confucius
It teaches through humorous, strange stories instead of terse verse
It is a list of rituals
check.why: The Daodejing speaks in compressed verse; the Zhuangzi tells stories of butterflies, cooks, trees and arguments.

lessons.title: Death, Usefulness and Freedom
lessons.mainIdea: The Zhuangzi treats death as part of nature's transformations and praises the freedom of those who stop chasing usefulness, status and fixed opinions.
reading: When Zhuangzi's wife died, the story goes, his friend Huizi came to offer condolences and found Zhuangzi sitting on the ground, drumming on a basin and singing. Huizi was shocked. Zhuangzi explained that at first he grieved like anyone. Then he reflected that before her birth she had no life, no form and no breath. Within the great mix of things a change produced breath, breath produced form, and form produced life. Now another change had brought death, like the passing of the four seasons. To keep wailing, he said, would show he did not understand fate.

Set that beside the Confucian rites of the last chapter, with three years of mourning for a parent. Confucians saw careful mourning as the proper expression of love and a support of social order. The Zhuangzi pokes at ritual that has become mere form and treats death as one more *transformation* in nature's endless changes. Neither view dismisses grief; they differ about what grief should become. Chinese families have often drawn on both, and on Buddhist rites, at the same funeral.

Zhuangzi also questions the value of being useful. In one story a carpenter passes a huge, gnarled oak that crowds admire and he ignores: its wood is worthless for boats, coffins or doors. That night the tree appears in his dream and asks whether he would rather it be useful, like fruit trees whose branches are stripped and broken every year. Its *uselessness* is what let it grow so large and live so long. Zhuangzi pushes readers to ask whose purposes usefulness serves.

The book's ideal is *free and easy wandering*, the title of its first chapter. Its heroes include the *hermit*, the craftsman and the oddball who has stepped outside the race for office. When messengers from a ruler invited Zhuangzi to take high office, he supposedly replied that he would rather be a live turtle dragging its tail in the mud than a dead one honored in a palace shrine. Many readers found in these stories a freedom that shaped Chinese poets, painters and hermits for two thousand years.

words.d: a change from one form into another; the Zhuangzi treats both birth and death this way
in the Zhuangzi, being of no use to others' purposes, which can protect a thing and let it flourish
the title of the Zhuangzi's first chapter and its ideal of a life unbound by status and fixed opinions
a person who withdraws from society to live simply, often in the mountains; admired in Daoist writing

look.title: Two Requests for One Funeral
look.text: A grandfather in a Chinese American family has died. His eldest son wants the Confucian customs: white mourning clothes, offerings before an ancestral tablet, and a long period of restraint. But the grandfather asked, before he died, that no one wail for long. He quoted Zhuangzi drumming on a basin and asked for music at his funeral. Both requests come from love.
look.prompt: What does each side believe grief should do? Could the family honor both requests at once, and what would that look like?

check.q: What was Zhuangzi doing when Huizi came after the death of Zhuangzi's wife?
choices: Drumming on a basin and singing

lessons.title: Celestial Masters and Daoist Priests
lessons.mainIdea: From the second century CE, Daoism also became an organized religion with revealed scriptures, ordained priests, temples, monasteries and a vast canon.
reading: In 142 CE, according to Daoist tradition, a man named *Zhang Daoling* was on a mountain in Sichuan when Laozi appeared to him as the divine Taishang Laojun and made him the first Celestial Master. Zhang organized communities whose members gave five pecks of rice a year, confessed their wrongs and sought healing through ritual. The movement, the Way of the *Celestial Masters*, is the root of organized Daoist religion. Its leaders passed the title through Zhang's descendants, and in 1949 the Celestial Master of the day moved to Taiwan.

Scholars once sharply divided philosophical Daoism, the Daodejing and Zhuangzi, from religious Daoism, with its gods, priests and rites. Many now find that line too sharp. Religious Daoists read the Daodejing as scripture, and in 166 CE the Han emperor Huan offered sacrifice to Laozi in his own palace, after sending officials to Laozi's reputed birthplace the year before. New revealed scriptures followed in the fourth and fifth centuries from schools such as Highest Clarity and Numinous Treasure. Under the Tang dynasty, whose emperors claimed descent from Laozi because they shared his surname Li, Daoism enjoyed imperial favor.

Two main orders exist today. Zhengyi, Orthodox Unity, descends from the Celestial Masters; its priests may marry and live at home, performing rituals for families and communities. *Quanzhen*, Complete Perfection, founded by Wang Chongyang in the 1160s, is monastic: its monks and nuns are celibate, avoid meat and alcohol, and live in temples such as the White Cloud Temple in Beijing. A *daoshi*, a Daoist priest, leads rituals of offering, purification, healing and funerals, often with chanting, drums, incense and embroidered robes.

The *Daoist Canon*, the Daozang, collects the tradition's writings. The standard edition, printed in 1445 under the Ming dynasty, holds about 1,400 works: scriptures, commentaries, ritual manuals, medical and alchemical texts and histories. Like the Buddhist canon, it is less a single book than a library. In the twentieth century Daoism suffered heavily, especially during the Cultural Revolution, when temples were closed and priests sent home. Today it is one of the five officially recognized religions in the People's Republic of China, and it is active in China, Taiwan and overseas.

words.d: the founder, in Daoist tradition, of the Celestial Masters movement after a revelation from Laozi in 142 CE
the first organized Daoist religious movement, founded in the second century CE; its line continues in Zhengyi Daoism
Complete Perfection, a monastic Daoist order founded in the 1160s whose monks and nuns are celibate

lessons.title: Immortals, Qi and Inner Alchemy
lessons.mainIdea: Many Daoists have sought long life and transcendence, first through elixirs and later through inner alchemy, the refining of the body's own energies.
reading: Chinese paintings often show the *Eight Immortals*, a band of figures who each carry a symbol, such as a fan, a sword, a gourd, a flower basket or a flute. They are *xian*, immortals or transcendents, people said to have perfected themselves until they no longer die in the ordinary way. Stories of xian living on far mountains or islands are older than organized Daoism, and emperors sent expeditions to find them. According to Sima Qian, the First Emperor of Qin sent a large party across the sea to seek the elixir of immortality.

One early method was *outer alchemy*: preparing elixirs from minerals such as cinnabar, which contains mercury, and from gold. The practice produced real chemical knowledge; Chinese alchemists are often credited with the experiments that led to gunpowder. It also caused deaths, and historians believe several Tang emperors died from elixir poisoning. Over time many Daoists turned the language of the furnace and the cauldron inward.

*Inner alchemy*, neidan, treats the body itself as the laboratory. Through breathing exercises, visualization, diet and meditation, the practitioner refines three treasures: jing, essence; *qi*, vital energy or breath; and shen, spirit. Qi is a central idea across Chinese thought: the energy that flows through the body and through all of nature. Teachers of inner alchemy describe the goal in different ways, from a long and healthy life to the birth of an immortal spirit body. Quanzhen made inner alchemy the core of its monastic practice.

How should a student read these claims? As with any tradition, describe what practitioners believe and do, and attribute it. Some Daoists understand immortality literally, others as a symbol of union with the Dao, and many ordinary temple visitors seek health and blessing rather than immortality. Compare other traditions' hopes about what lies beyond death: resurrection in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, moksha in Hinduism, nirvana in Buddhism. A later unit of this course returns to that comparison.

words.d: a popular group of Daoist immortals, each shown with a symbol, common in Chinese art and stories
an immortal or transcendent; in Daoist belief, a person perfected beyond ordinary death
the attempt to make elixirs of long life from minerals such as cinnabar and gold

look.title: Before Dawn in a Monastery
look.text: A Quanzhen nun rises before dawn and sits in stillness. She breathes slowly into her lower belly and pictures qi circling up her spine and down the front of her body. Later she chants scriptures with the other nuns, eats a meal without meat and tends the temple garden. Asked what she is doing, she says she is returning to the Dao.

lessons.title: The Three Teachings and Popular Religion
lessons.mainIdea: In Chinese life Daoism, Confucianism and Buddhism have long mixed with local gods and ancestor rites, so most people drew on all three rather than joining one.
reading: Walk into a busy temple in Taiwan and you may find, on different altars, the Buddhist bodhisattva Guanyin, the sea goddess *Mazu*, the red-faced general Guandi, and Laozi. Worshipers move from altar to altar with incense sticks, bow, drop a donation in a box, and ask for help with exams, health or business. Some drop a pair of crescent-shaped wooden blocks to receive a yes or no answer. This is *Chinese popular religion*: the everyday practice of most Chinese people through history, with no single founder, scripture or membership.

Popular religion pictures an unseen world organized a little like the old imperial government. At the top sits the *Jade Emperor*. City Gods act as local magistrates of the spirit world. The *Kitchen God*, whose picture hangs by the stove, is said to report on the family to heaven just before the Lunar New Year, so families offer him sweets. Daoist priests often serve as ritual experts for this world, Buddhist monks commonly chant at funerals, and Confucian ideals shape the family's ancestor rites.

The three teachings, met in the last chapter, grew together over centuries. When Buddhism arrived from India in the first centuries CE, translators borrowed Daoist words to explain it, and scholars see Daoist influence in Chan Buddhism, called Zen in Japan. Emperors sometimes favored one teaching and restricted another, yet a common saying held that the three teachings are one. Scholars call such blending *syncretism*. A traditional painting subject, the vinegar tasters, shows Confucius, the Buddha and Laozi around a jar of vinegar, each reacting differently.

Chinese communities abroad carry these practices with them. In Chicago's Chinatown and in Chinese, Taiwanese and Vietnamese homes across the United States, families light incense at home altars, celebrate the Lunar New Year and honor ancestors. Surveys have trouble counting Daoists for the same reason they cannot count Confucians: most practitioners do not think of themselves as belonging to one religion. The question a scholar asks here is less which religion are you, and more which practices do you keep, and why.

words.d: the everyday religious practice of most Chinese people, mixing local gods, ancestors and the three teachings
a sea goddess honored in many temples in Taiwan and coastal China as a protector of sailors

look.title: The Vinegar Tasters
look.text: In the traditional scene, three old men stand around a jar of vinegar. Confucius tastes it and makes a sour face. The Buddha tastes it and finds it bitter. Laozi tastes it and smiles. One common modern reading says the scene takes a Daoist view: to Confucians life needs correcting, to Buddhists life is suffering, and to Daoists life is good as it is.
look.prompt: Whose point of view does this reading of the scene take? How might a Confucian or a Buddhist painter have shown the same three figures, and what would each want viewers to notice?

lessons.title: The Way in Brush, Body and Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: Daoist ideas of qi, yin and yang and harmony with nature shaped Chinese landscape painting, traditional medicine and martial arts such as tai chi.
reading: In Fan Kuan's Travelers Among Mountains and Streams, painted around 1000 CE in the Song dynasty, a great cliff fills most of the silk. Near the bottom, so small you might miss them, a few travelers drive their mules along a path. *Landscape painting*, called shanshui, mountain-water, pictured human beings as a small part of a vast, living nature. Many such painters were scholar-officials painting in their leisure, and the empty space in their work, mist and sky, echoes the Daodejing's praise of emptiness.

*Traditional Chinese medicine* grew from the same ideas. Its classic text, the Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, compiled in the Han era, describes health as a balance of yin and yang and a smooth flow of qi along channels in the body. Practitioners use herbs, acupuncture, diet and exercise to restore balance. Hospitals in China often offer it alongside modern medicine. Researchers continue to test which treatments work, with mixed results so far, so a careful student describes it as a healing tradition and lets evidence judge specific claims.

*Tai chi*, taijiquan, is a slow, flowing martial art now practiced by millions for health. Its movements shift weight between empty and full, soft and firm, in the pattern of yin and yang. Legend credits a Daoist of the *Wudang Mountains*, Zhang Sanfeng; historians trace the known styles to the Chen family village in Henan in the seventeenth century. Either way, the art applies the Daodejing's teaching that the soft overcomes the hard: a skilled practitioner yields to force and redirects it. The Wudang temples are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Daoist words have also traveled into English, sometimes far from their roots. Yin and yang appear in advertisements, and the Tao of this or that is a common book title. A careful student notices when an idea is being borrowed and asks what it meant at home. In parks from Beijing to Chicago, people practice tai chi each morning, many of them without any religious commitment. The practice shows how a tradition's ideas can live in art, medicine and movement well beyond its temples.

a healing tradition based on balancing yin and yang and the flow of qi, using herbs, acupuncture and diet

look.title: The Soft and the Stiff
look.text: When people are born they are soft and supple; when they die they are stiff and hard. Grass and trees are tender and pliant while they live, and dry and brittle when they die. So the stiff and hard are companions of death, and the soft and supple are companions of life. A rigid army will not win; a stiff tree will be cut down.

look.prompt: How might a tai chi teacher use this chapter to explain the art? Where else, in sports or in arguments, does the supple beat the stiff, and where might it not?
